Tide tables are published predictions of when high and low tides will occur at a given location, along with the water height at each moment. They are calculated from long records of sea level and from the known movements of the Moon and Sun, which drive the rise and fall of the ocean. Because these movements repeat in predictable cycles, the tables can be produced years in advance with remarkable accuracy.

Each entry in a table gives a time and a height, and the height is measured against a chart datum. This reference level is usually set near the lowest tide expected at a site, so that the water almost never falls below it and the printed heights stay positive. Heights are often given in metres or feet, so it is worth checking the unit before relying on any figure.

Tide tables also reflect the phases of the Moon. Spring tides, with the largest range between high and low water, occur near new and full moons when the Sun and Moon pull in line. Neap tides, with smaller ranges, occur near the quarter moons when they pull at right angles. Tables therefore show clear patterns across each fortnight, which helps sailors, anglers and coastal walkers plan around the strongest and weakest tidal flows.

Tables are not the whole story, because weather can shift the actual water level. A strong offshore wind or a low-pressure system can raise or lower the sea by a noticeable amount, and the tables do not account for this. Shallow estuaries and harbours may also run earlier or later than the published times suggest. For that reason, a careful mariner compares the tables with local observations and current forecasts before committing to a course of action near the shore, since the printed figures are predictions rather than guarantees.
